subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 45-year-old man has his blood pressure measured during a routine visit: 130/90 mm Hg. His physician notes the systolic and diastolic values while discussing arterial mechanics.
question: What is this patient's pulse pressure?
explanation_correct: Pulse pressure = systolic blood pressure − diastolic blood pressure = 130 − 90 = 40 mm Hg. Pulse pressure is directly proportional to stroke volume and inversely proportional to arterial compliance.

explanation_incorrect.A: 110 mm Hg is the unweighted average of the systolic and diastolic pressures — that approximates mean arterial pressure, not pulse pressure.
explanation_incorrect.B: 1.44 is the systolic-to-diastolic ratio (130/90); pulse pressure is a difference, not a ratio.
explanation_incorrect.C: 220 mm Hg is the sum of the systolic and diastolic pressures; pulse pressure is their difference.
explanation_incorrect.D: 20 mm Hg results from halving the systolic-diastolic difference; the pulse pressure is the full difference (130 − 90 = 40).

educationalObjective: Pulse pressure = SBP − DBP, and it is directly proportional to stroke volume and inversely proportional to arterial compliance.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 24-year-old tall, thin man presents with dyspnea. His pulses are bounding and rapidly rising ('water-hammer' quality), and his blood pressure is 170/50 mm Hg. Auscultation reveals a blowing, early-diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border.
question: Which mechanism best explains this patient's wide pulse pressure?

options.text: Decreased arterial compliance from age-related aortic stiffening
Decreased stroke volume from advanced heart failure
Increased stroke volume ejected through an incompetent aortic valve with diastolic runoff back into the left ventricle
Impeded systolic ejection across a stenotic aortic valve
Increased systemic vascular resistance elevating diastolic pressure

explanation_correct: Pulse pressure is directly proportional to stroke volume and inversely proportional to arterial compliance. In aortic regurgitation, the left ventricle ejects a large stroke volume in systole, and in diastole blood regurgitates back through the incompetent valve into the ventricle, causing diastolic pressure to fall precipitously — producing a wide pulse pressure (170/50) with bounding, water-hammer pulses.

explanation_incorrect.A: Aortic stiffening decreases compliance and raises pulse pressure in older adults with isolated systolic hypertension, but this young patient has a normal-compliance aorta and valvular regurgitation instead.
explanation_incorrect.B: Decreased stroke volume lowers pulse pressure, as in advanced heart failure, cardiogenic shock, or tamponade — the opposite of this patient's wide pulse pressure.
explanation_incorrect.D: Impeded ejection across a stenotic aortic valve decreases stroke volume and narrows pulse pressure (aortic stenosis); this patient's murmur is diastolic, not systolic.
explanation_incorrect.E: Elevated systemic vascular resistance raises diastolic pressure and would narrow, not widen, the pulse pressure.

educationalObjective: Pulse pressure widens in aortic regurgitation because a large stroke volume is ejected while diastolic runoff lowers DBP; PP ∝ SV and ∝ 1/arterial compliance.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: An 80-year-old man is evaluated for exertional syncope. His carotid upstroke is slow and delayed (pulsus parvus et tardus), a harsh systolic ejection murmur is heard at the right second intercostal space radiating to the carotids, and his blood pressure is 110/95 mm Hg.
question: Which mechanism best explains this patient's narrow pulse pressure?

options.text: Age-related aortic stiffening decreasing arterial compliance
Reduced stroke volume from obstructed ejection across the stenotic aortic valve
Increased sympathetic tone raising diastolic pressure
A high-output state such as anemia increasing stroke volume
Diastolic runoff into the left ventricle lowering diastolic pressure

explanation_correct: Pulse pressure is directly proportional to stroke volume. In aortic stenosis, ejection across the narrowed valve is impeded, stroke volume falls, and the pulse pressure narrows (110/95 here), accompanied by the slow, delayed carotid upstroke of pulsus parvus et tardus. Narrow pulse pressure also occurs in cardiogenic shock, cardiac tamponade, and advanced heart failure — all states of reduced effective stroke volume.

explanation_incorrect.A: Decreased arterial compliance (aortic stiffening) increases pulse pressure, producing isolated systolic hypertension in older adults — the opposite finding.
explanation_incorrect.C: Increased sympathetic tone (eg, obstructive sleep apnea) is a mechanism of widened, not narrowed, pulse pressure.
explanation_incorrect.D: High-output states (eg, anemia, hyperthyroidism) increase stroke volume and widen pulse pressure.
explanation_incorrect.E: Diastolic runoff through an incompetent valve lowers DBP and widens pulse pressure (aortic regurgitation); this patient has stenosis, not regurgitation.

educationalObjective: Pulse pressure narrows in aortic stenosis, cardiogenic shock, cardiac tamponade, and advanced heart failure — all states of reduced stroke volume.
